item.title: What America Looks Like After 700 Meters of Sea Level Rise
item.summary: Ever wondered what North America would look like if the oceans rose by a staggering 690 meters? The Sliding Shores map gives us a fascinating peek at a radically transformed United States. Granted, even if every global ice sheet melted tomorrow, sea levels would max out around 80 meters - meaning this apocalyptic drowning is strictly theoretical. But as an exercise in extreme topographic visualization, it makes for a captivating spatial experiment. If you’re looking to explore actual, science-backed climate projections rather than wild cartographic extremes, Climate Central's Coastal Risk Finder is probably a better sea level rise map. However, Sliding Shores does offer a more dynamic, global perspective by rendering the entire planet as a 3D interactive globe rather than as a flat 2D map. Rather than sticking strictly to realistic sea level forecasts, the map features 16 pre-set, extreme planetary scenarios - ranging from catastrophic rises like total ice sheet melt (+70m) or drowning Mt. Everest (+8,849m), down to dramatic ocean drop-offs like the Last Ice Age coastline (-120m) or draining the oceans entirely (-11,000m). Read the original article at ${post.title} on ${blog.title}

The tool has 16 preset scenarios, from draining the oceans entirely (-11,000 m) and the Last Ice Age coastline (-120 m) to total ice sheet melt (+70 m) and drowning Mt. Everest (+8,849 m). Maps Mania stresses that the 690 m scenario is purely theoretical, as melting every ice sheet would raise sea level by only around 80 m.

item.title: Earth from Space: West Antarctica
item.summary: Image: This image over part of West Antarctica was captured by Copernicus Sentinel-3 on 30 September 2026.
item.page_text:
You have already liked this page, you can only like it once!
This image over part of West Antarctica was captured by Copernicus Sentinel-3 on 30 September 2026.
Zoom in to explore this image at its full resolution.
At this time of year, winter is coming to an end in the southern hemisphere and the sea ice is at its annual maximum extent. It reaches as far as the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula, visible in the central part of the image, where there is also some cloud coverage.
An area of about 1200 km by 1700 km is shown – this area is on the periphery of the Antarctic continent, which is about 4500 km across its main landmass. Elephant Island, about 50 km in length, is clearly visible against ice-free ocean on the left-hand side of the image. It is about 930 km from the tip of Argentina’s Tierra del Fuego, which is not pictured.
Sea ice for Antarctica’s winter season most likely peaked on 14 September 2026, according to the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC). This image shows sea ice engulfing the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula as well as part of the Weddell Sea, east of the peninsula.
White cloud covers much of the lower part of the image but sea ice is clearly visible in the upper-right area. A variety of textures reflect the different types of ice, including areas of tightly packed sea ice on the right. Large floes comparable in size to Elephant Island are visible and these progress to much smaller pieces of sea ice that form swirling shapes in the ocean.

draft.what_it_shows: A Copernicus Sentinel-3 image of part of West Antarctica captured on 30 September 2026, covering about 1200 km by 1700 km around the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula and part of the Weddell Sea. Sea ice is near its annual maximum (NSIDC says it most likely peaked on 14 September 2026). Textures range from tightly packed ice on the right to large floes comparable to the 50 km-long Elephant Island and smaller swirling pieces, with cloud over much of the lower part and some cloud near the peninsula tip.

Antarctic sea ice most likely peaked on 14 September 2026, according to NSIDC. On 30 September, Copernicus Sentinel-3 caught it engulfing the tip of the Antarctic Peninsula.

The @esa scene spans about 1200 km by 1700 km: tightly packed ice, floes as large as 50 km-long Elephant Island and smaller pieces swirling in the ocean.
